summary:
Measured every brain subcommand (5 runs, median) in scratch copies, then grew the state synthetically. Nothing was written to /home/user/Claude-Brain; every scratch copy had its git remote removed before use.

Headline numbers:
- **Speed floor is start-up, not work.** In a fresh clone every call costs about 240 ms, because `bin/brain` forbids a bytecode cache and imports all 21 modules. A prototype (cache outside the tree, import only the module that owns the command) gives 54-78 ms with identical output, and all 410 tests pass.
- **Output is small and bounded.** Boot is 311-985 B across modes, and stays at 939 B with 300 requirements and 300 recorded sessions. The waste is in what the bytes say:
  - The failure digest of `brain run` shows the first three lines that match a loose word list. On a 2,000-line npm/jest log it printed 744 B without one line about the failing test.
  - On "Continue", 479 of boot's 985 B are recall hits matched on the trigger word.
  - Help and usage errors cost 250-3,553 B each.
- **Three cliffs with scale.**
  - `plan schedule` takes 85 s for 200 tickets, against 0.26 s without annealing and with byte-identical output.
  - `learn consolidate` goes from 0.8 s to 9.9 s when memory grows from 141 to 2,000 items; a one-decorator fix brings it to 1.0 s with the same operations.
  - Recall is linear, but 80% of its time is Python stemming of the whole memory on every call (1.0 s per call at 10,000 items).
- **Flat with scale:** boot, resume, status, checkpoint, req, ml and hr reports, and both hooks.

Several things I measured are already in the live `docs/plan/IMPROVEMENT_PLAN.md`; I did not spend finding slots on them, and the confirming numbers are in `data`: the 400-item deadlock (learning-09), `brain run` losing everything when the tool times out (quality-path-05), `hr report` asking to consolidate folded hires (owner-docs-13), the unenforced 3,200-token total (core-14), and Spanish recall (e2e-trial-09). Findings 4 and 5 overlap plan items core-13, instructions-04 and e2e-trial-20 and add byte counts and exact lines.

Call frequencies in the token ranking are assumptions anchored on the plan's own trial (11 build commands, 36 process commands, 5 help look-ups for a three-item project); no real project session exists yet to measure them.
strengths: Boot is cheap and stays cheap: 311 B (brain only), 434 B (empty project), 985 B (managed, mid-item), capped at 1,500 B by a test. It was still 939 B and 125 ms with 300 requirement lines, 300 run records and 1,800 gate rows. Do not let new boot lines erode this.

State commands are bounded as a project grows. At 300 requirements: resume 960 B, status 534 B, checkpoint 123 B, req check capped at 20 lines (1,832 B). At 300 consolidated sessions: ml report 971 B, learn status 249 B, all about 140 ms.

The run-through-a-file design works on the success path: a 2,000-line log comes back as under 750 B with the full text on disk, and run logs are git-ignored so they never bloat the project repository.

Both hooks are cheap and fail open: the edit guard costs 26 ms per Edit/Write; the Stop hook took 216 ms on the real 24.7 MB session (main plus helpers) and 637 ms on a synthetic 110 MB transcript, linear at about 5 ms per MB. Boot with the daily news check due took 0.75 s, and 0.17 s with a dead proxy.

The loaded text is compact: about 2,550 tokens always loaded (CLAUDE.md 5,423 B of a 6,000 B cap), skill bodies 484-705 tokens each, agent files 341-419 tokens, and a helper brief is a 2.4 KB file pointed at by one line. Consolidating 1,800 records from 300 sessions took 0.35 s.

findings.title: The failure digest of `brain run` often omits the cause, so the lead has to open the log
findings.evidence:
engine/gate.py:57 `for i in hits[:3]:  # the first failures are usually the cause`, where hits are lines matching ERROR_RE (gate.py:23: error|fail|exception|traceback|assert|undefined...). Four cases run through `brain run` (paths normalised to /home/user/trip-planner):
(1) A 2,000-line, 67,732 B npm ci + jest log with one failing test near line 1,180 -> 744 B printed: `npm warn deprecated domexception@4.0.0...`, `npm warn deprecated abab@2.0.6...`, `.../src/lib/errorMessages.ts`, `14:7  warning  'fallbackError' is assigned...`, then six `npm error workspace/location/command...` lines. The failing suite (FlightList.test.tsx, 'sorts flights by price', line 27) does not appear. Reading the log whole would cost about 16,900 tokens.
(2) unittest with 2 failures and 1 error (41 lines) -> 618 B: `ERROR: test_cheapest_empty`, a 70-dash rule, `Traceback (most recent call last):`, one File line, `...`, then `AssertionError: 5 != '5 EUR'` (another test, unnamed). Missing: `ValueError: min() iterable argument is empty` and the names test_sorted_by_price and test_total_with_currency. 3 of 12 body lines are rules or blank.
(3) tsc build, 3 type errors then 1,970 noise lines -> 721 B: the errors are shown, but 9 of 16 lines are blanks, `...` and npm boilerplate.
(4) Chained Python traceback (71 lines) -> 682 B: both exceptions shown, but not the frame that raised the first (`line 8, in price_of`).
Prototype (tools/digest_proto.py, about 45 lines, standard library): npm 537 B with `FAIL src/components/FlightList.test.tsx`, the test title, `> 27 | expect(cities).toEqual(...)` and `FlightList.test.tsx:27:20`; unittest 870 B with all three tests, each with innermost frame and exception line; tsc 597 B; crash 385 B with `line 8, in price_of` and both exceptions. The prototype still shows two noise lines in the tsc case and miscounts hidden lines, so treat the byte figures as indicative.
findings.proposed_fix:
Replace 'first three regex hits plus tail' in run_filtered with:
(a) Before matching, drop lines that cannot be the cause (npm warn/notice, PASS, lines starting with a tick, lint warnings) and decoration (rules of -=~^, blank lines, `Traceback (most recent call last):`, npm error code/path/workspace/location/command lines).
(b) Match failure shapes instead of words: `FAIL|FAILED|ERROR` headers, jest bullet and cross lines, `error TSnnnn` and `file:line: error`, a line that starts with an exception class, pytest `E   ` lines, the jest `> NN |` frame, the first `at file:line:col`.
(c) For each Python traceback keep the innermost File line, its code line and the exception line.
(d) De-duplicate, keep the 12-line cap, end with `... N more failure lines in the log`.
(e) Strip the working directory from paths and print the log path relative to it.
Keep `--tail`. Store the four logs as fixtures.
findings.acceptance: A new test feeds four fixture logs (unittest with three failing tests; jest failure inside 2,000 lines; three tsc errors inside 2,000 lines; chained Python traceback). For each it asserts: digest is at most 900 B; it contains every failing test or file name and its assertion or exception line; no line starts with `npm warn`; no line consists only of -, =, ~ or spaces. `test_run_output_is_capped_and_keeps_quoting` still passes.

findings.title: `plan schedule` takes 85 s on 200 tickets for the same answer it gives in 0.26 s
findings.evidence:
engine/schedule.py:304-306 `return min(3000, max(300, 60 * n))` iterations, each calling decode(), which rescans every placed ticket for every candidate start. Measured on the same synthetic plan cut to size (4 agents, seed 0):

| tickets | with annealing | --no-anneal | makespan gain |
|---|---|---|---|
| 14 | 0.34 s | 0.26 s | none |
| 28 | 0.24 s | 0.20 s | none (already at lower bound) |
| 50 | 2.90 s | 0.28 s | 715 -> 690 (3.5%) |
| 75 | 8.78 s | 0.23 s | 1060 -> 1040 (1.9%) |
| 100 | 15.57 s | 0.25 s | 1410 -> 1395 (1.1%) |
| 150 | 40.02 s | 0.35 s | 2370 -> 2355 (0.6%) |
| 200 | 85.0 s (median of 3) | 0.26 s | none; output byte-identical, 605 B, `method: critical-path` |

Time grows about n^2.4 once the iteration cap is reached at 50 tickets. At roughly 230 tickets the command would pass the Bash tool's 120 s default and be killed with nothing printed.
findings.proposed_fix: Bound annealing by work, not only by count: `iters = min(3000, max(300, 60*n), 4_000_000 // (n*n))`. That leaves plans up to 36 tickets unchanged and gives 1,600 iterations at 50, 400 at 100, 100 at 200. Skip annealing when the critical-path makespan is within 1% of the lower bound (today it skips only on an exact match). Keep it deterministic (no clock). Optionally make decode cheaper by keeping placed tickets sorted by finish time.
findings.acceptance: `brain plan schedule` on the 200-ticket fixture finishes in under 3 s, and at every size its makespan is no worse than the critical-path makespan. The existing brute-force comparison (25 of 25 small plans) and `test_same_seed_same_schedule_where_annealing_runs` still pass. A new test asserts `iterations_for(n) * n * n <= 4_000_000` for n above 36.

findings.title: Every brain call costs about 240 ms in a fresh clone: no bytecode cache, and all 21 modules imported for any command
findings.evidence:
bin/brain:10 `sys.dont_write_bytecode = True`; bin/brain:19-23 imports every module in MODULES; engine/gate.py:16-17 import urllib at module top. `__pycache__/` is already git-ignored, so a cloud session (fresh clone) never has a cache unless someone runs the brain's own tests.
`python3 -X importtime bin/brain boot`: 184 modules; top-level imports total 85 ms, of which urllib.request 22.6 ms (http.client 20.3, email.parser 8.6, ssl 6.7), engine.common 11.7, argparse 10.4, concurrent.futures 4.5, engine.state 3.7 (subprocess 3.2), statistics 2.6, shutil 2.2, ast 2.2, xml.etree 2.1. Bare `python3 -c pass` is 17.5 ms.
Median of 9 runs, managed scratch project, output and exit code identical in all three columns:

| command | as shipped, fresh clone | + bytecode cache outside the tree | + import only the owning module |
|---|---|---|---|
| boot | 237 ms | 118 ms | 54 ms |
| boot Continue | 251 | 135 | 76 |
| run -- true | 250 | 132 | 56 |
| checkpoint | 238 | 119 | 58 |
| resume | 256 | 132 | 56 |
| recall | 253 | 142 | 78 |
| req check | 237 | 128 | 45 |
| hr hire --dry-run | 255 | 122 | 77 |

After all runs: 0 `__pycache__` directories inside the repository. The full suite passes on the prototype: `Ran 410 tests in 34.118s OK`. Absolute saving is modest: about 9 s over the 47 commands of the plan's three-item trial.
findings.proposed_fix:
(1) Bytecode: replace line 10 with `sys.pycache_prefix = <user cache dir>/claude-brain/pyc` (the tree stays pristine, also on a read-only checkout), or simply delete the line since `__pycache__/` is ignored. Do the same in the two hooks.
(2) Lazy dispatch: add a `COMMANDS = {command: module}` table to engine/__init__.py. In bin/brain, when argv[0] is in the table, import and register only that module; fall back to all modules for `--help`, an unknown command or a failed import. A test asserts the table equals what the register() functions actually add, so it cannot drift.
(3) Move `import urllib.error, urllib.request` in gate.py into check_live.
findings.acceptance: In a fresh clone, the median of 9 `brain boot` runs after the first is at most 100 ms on this container (237 ms today) and `git status --short` in the brain stays empty. `python3 -X importtime bin/brain run -- true` lists neither urllib.request nor ssl. The table-equals-registered test passes. The full suite, `brain doctor` and `brain lint` pass.

findings.title: Frequent commands print bytes the lead cannot use: log path on every success, blank lines, duplicated lines
findings.evidence:
Byte counts with paths normalised to /home/user/trip-planner.
- `brain run -- true` -> 106 B: `ok in 0.0s · 0 lines · full output: /home/user/trip-planner/.brain/log/run/20261110-180921-b5bea41b.log`. 85 of the 106 B are the label and an absolute path nobody opens after a pass.
- `brain run` on a passing unittest -> 138 B: the same header, then `  Ran 2 tests in 0.000s`, a blank line, `  OK`.
- `brain gate` passing -> 225 B (same header and blank line).
- `brain hr hire` -> 764 B, 7 lines. The brief path is printed twice (`brief:` and inside `delegate with:`). `role default: 0 of 3 safe arms have 8+ outcomes (0 pooled); learning needs 2` and `size band L (no settled hires yet)` are learner internals. `note: the brief is 372 words; briefs read best under 350` is about a brief the engine itself wrote.
- `brain req check` prints two lines for one id: ` - R-004: no 'passes when' (how will this be checked?)` and ` - R-004: open — I want it in Spanish and English`.
- `brain req list` on a 300-line ledger prints the first 15 rows, all `[done]`, 2,444 B (611 tokens), before any open line.
Ranking (tokens per call x assumed calls for a three-item project; counts anchored on the plan's trial of 11 build and 36 process commands and 5 help look-ups): help 5 x ~200 = 1,000; run 8 ok x 34 + 3 failed x 170 = 782; hr hire 2 x 191 = 382; recall 2 x 160 = 320; boot 246; req check 2 x 107 = 214; gate 3 x 56 = 168; checkpoint 4 x 40 = 160. Total about 3,600 tokens.
findings.proposed_fix:
- run and gate on success: print `ok in 0.1s · 5 lines` plus the last non-blank output line, with no log path. Keep the path on failure, relative to the working directory, labelled `log:`. Never print blank lines in the digest. Expected: 138 -> about 45 B; `run -- true` 106 -> about 21 B; gate 225 -> about 130 B.
- hr hire: one `brief:` line, keep the `delegate with:` line with the path once, move the learner-basis and size-band text to `--json`, drop the word-count note. Expected: 764 -> about 430 B.
- req check: one line per id (`R-004: open, no 'passes when' — ...`).
- req list: show open lines first by default; add `--all` for the rest.
findings.acceptance: Byte-cap tests in the style of the boot cap: `run -- true` at most 40 B; a passing run at most 80 B plus its last output line, with no '/' path in it; a failing run's header contains a path that does not start with '/'; `hr hire` at most 500 B on the fixture and the brief path appears once outside the delegate line; `req check` prints each id once; `req list` on a ledger with done and open lines prints an open line first. `brain lint` still passes (no flag removed).

findings.title: On resume, half of boot's output is recall matched on the trigger word (adds numbers to plan items core-13 and instructions-04)
findings.evidence:
engine/detect.py:131 `hits = recall.recall(request, family=family, k=3, budget_tokens=260, ...)` passes the owner's words, so for a resume the query is the trigger itself.
`brain boot "Continue"` in a managed project mid-item -> 985 B, of which the three recall lines are 479 B (49%): `[own-trigger-words] Short triggers such as "set up", "Start running" and "Continue" start or resume the whole protocol...`, `[rule-checkpoint-boundary] Write the state file at every item boundary...` (CLAUDE.md rule 7 says the same), `[pref-visible-progress]`. Brain-only it is 479 of 861 B (56%).
- `boot "Keep going"` returns `own-decide-and-record`, `sw-tag-known-good`, `pref-phone-short`.
- `boot "Continúa"` and `boot "Sigue"` return no recall line at all, so the block is evidently not needed to resume.
- Recall on the recorded item, next items and notes returned `nothing relevant in memory`.
Each of these recalls is also appended to `.brain/log/recall.jsonl`, the record that decides which items may earn credit, so the same three generic items are logged as shown on every resume.
findings.proposed_fix: In boot_lines, when the route's task class is `resume`, build the recall query from the state (item, next list, notes) instead of the request, and print nothing when recall is silent. Mark items whose text restates the always-loaded file (a boolean field such as `in_core`, set through the pipeline) and let boot skip them; ids stay, so the golden set is untouched. Do not log a boot recall that printed nothing.
findings.acceptance: On the fixture project, `brain boot "Continue"` is at most 520 B and contains none of own-trigger-words, rule-checkpoint-boundary, pref-visible-progress. With a state item that matches a playbook line (for example a deploy item) the matching item is shown. `boot "Continúa"` and `boot "Continue"` print the same lines. The existing boot cap tests pass.

findings.title: Consolidation re-tokenises both texts four times for every note-item pair: 0.8 s becomes 9.9 s at 2,000 items
findings.evidence:
engine/learn.py:500-518: `restates()` calls jaccard() and containment(), and each calls `_core()` on both texts; engine/learn.py:992 runs it for every live item per note.
`brain learn consolidate --dry-run` with 500 inbox records (50 sessions, 100 notes):
- 141 items: 824 ms (median of 5)
- 2,000 items: 9,884 ms (median of 3)
cProfile at 2,000 items: 200,952 restates calls -> 803,840 `_core` calls -> 803,940 `common.words` calls, about 98% of the run.
With `@functools.lru_cache(maxsize=65536)` on `_core` returning a frozenset (a 4-line diff): 0.91-1.02 s, and the delta has the same operation counts (`ADD 45, APPEND_STAT 51, INC_HARMFUL 43, INC_HELPFUL 95, MARK_INBOX 52, ML_FOLD 1, SET_STATUS 58`). On clean state with the patch, `python3 -m unittest tests.test_learn tests.test_guard tests.test_rehearsal` -> `Ran 80 tests ... OK`.
The per-file budget of 400 items bounds memory at about 3,600 items, so the unpatched worst case is roughly 18 s per 100 notes.
findings.proposed_fix: Memoise `_core` (lru_cache, return a frozenset) so each distinct text is tokenised once per run. Optionally compute each note's word set once and skip items that share no word with it before calling restates.
findings.acceptance: A test builds a workspace with 2,000 items and 100 notes and asserts that `common.words` is called fewer than 5,000 times during build_consolidation (803,940 today), and that the resulting delta equals the one produced with the cache disabled. tests.test_learn and tests.test_rehearsal pass.
findings.repro: python3 .../performance/tools/gen_items.py <copy> 2000 && python3 .../performance/tools/gen_inbox.py <copy> 50 mixed10 && time python3 <copy>/bin/brain learn consolidate --dry-run

findings.title: Recall stems the whole memory in Python on every call: 80% of its time, linear in items
findings.evidence:
engine/recall.py:442 `doc_terms = [set(tokens(" ".join(_fields(i)))) for i in pool]` runs the pure-Python Porter stemmer over every item on every call; boot calls it too.
In-process, averaged over the 60 golden queries (select total / of which stemming):
- 141 items: 15.4 / 12.0 ms
- 2,000 items: 246.7 / 209.0 ms
- 10,000 items: 1,245.8 / 997.2 ms
Cold CLI call: recall 153 -> 282 -> 1,043 ms; `boot "Continue"` 136 -> 290 -> 1,003 ms.
Two-line prototype (`@functools.lru_cache` on `porter`, and stem only items whose BM25 relevance is above 0; an item with no query term has coverage 0, so results cannot change): identical ids and scores on all 60 queries on both paths at 141 and 2,000 items (`identical ids and scores on 60 queries x 2 paths: True`). Cold CLI: recall 134 / 198 / 547 ms; boot 122 / 181 / 471 ms. tests.test_recall passes on the patched copy (18 tests OK).
Quality under synthetic growth (distractors of random words, half from the items' own vocabulary and half from docs/, so harsher than real lessons): recall@5 0.781 -> 0.478 -> 0.353 and MRR 0.830 -> 0.608 -> 0.465 at 141 / 2,000 / 10,000. Read that as a direction, not a forecast.
findings.proposed_fix: Apply the two-line change. If the item budget is ever raised, also cache `load_items` plus the tokenised fields by the item files' content hash through engine/cache.py; at 10,000 items load_items is 196 ms and the index build 82 ms per call.
findings.acceptance: A test asserts select() returns identical ids and scores with and without the change on the golden set, and that `porter` is called fewer than 3,000 times for one query over the real items. The golden regression test passes unchanged.

findings.title: Help pages and usage errors are among the largest outputs: 3,553 B for `--help`, 250-760 B per mistyped flag
findings.evidence:
Measured: `brain --help` 3,553 B (888 tokens; the 32-command list is printed twice before the per-command lines); `hr hire --help` 1,996 B; `close --help` 1,850 B; `learn note --help` 1,687 B. All 44 help pages sum to 25,217 B.
Usage errors print the whole usage block before the one line that matters: `brain hr hire` (missing task) 756 B; `brain close --outcome done` 628 B; `brain bogus` 608 B; `brain checkpoint --stage building` 519 B.
The lead's own transcript in this session shows eight help look-ups (hr hire, hr, learn, learn consolidate, ml, guard, radar, eval), and the plan's trial counted five on a three-item project.
Prototype (`metavar="<command>"` on the subparsers and a parser subclass whose error() prints one line; subparsers inherit the class): `--help` 3,553 -> 2,674 B; `hr hire` 756 -> 86 B (`brain hr hire: the following arguments are required: task (see: brain hr hire --help)`); `close --outcome done` 628 -> 122 B; `checkpoint --stage building` 519 -> 200 B; `req add` 252 -> 89 B; `bogus` 608 -> 383 B.
findings.proposed_fix: In bin/brain, pass `metavar="<command>"` to add_subparsers and use an ArgumentParser subclass whose `error()` writes `<prog>: <message> (see: <prog> --help)` and exits 2. For the two longest pages (`hr hire`, `close`), move rarely used flags into an argument group that prints only with `--help-all`, or shorten their help strings.
findings.acceptance: A test asserts `brain --help` is at most 2,800 B, a missing-argument error is one line of at most 120 B, and an invalid-choice error still names the valid choices. `brain lint` (which checks flags named in the instruction files) passes.

findings.title: The repo map's cache is defeated by the brain's own bookkeeping, and bookkeeping files are ranked as source (measurement and fix for open item M8)
findings.evidence:
engine/repomap.py:49-50 skips only `.brain/cache`, so the walk and the cache key include `.brain/log/run/*.log`, `.brain/STATE.md`, `STATUS.md` and the rest.
In the scratch project: `brain map` twice -> `(cached)`; after one `brain run -- true` -> `map: 12 of 52 files ...` not cached; after one `brain checkpoint` -> not cached again. During building the cache therefore never hits.
The output of that project's map: 11 of 12 lines are bookkeeping (`.brain/requirements.jsonl`, three `.brain/log/run/...log`, `NEEDS_YOU.md`, `STATUS.md`, `.brain/PLAN.md`, `.brain/STATE.md`, lessons, project.json, .gitignore) and 1 is source. In the larger project it walked 333 files, of which about 315 were run records and logs, and 4 of the 12 lines were bookkeeping.
Cost of a miss on a synthetic tree: 5,000 files 1,527 ms cold, 388 ms warm, 1,578 ms after editing one file; 1,000 files 468 / 295 / 492 ms. Linear, no cliff; output constant at about 1,000 B.
findings.proposed_fix: Skip the whole `.brain/` directory plus `STATUS.md` and `NEEDS_YOU.md` in walk(). When the root is a git work tree, take the file list from `git ls-files -co --exclude-standard`, which also removes generated and ignored files (the open M8 item). Cache per-file extraction by content hash so one edit re-parses one file.
findings.acceptance: A test in a managed fixture project asserts no printed map line starts with `.brain/` or is STATUS.md or NEEDS_YOU.md, and that `brain map` reports `(cached)` again after `brain run -- true` and after `brain checkpoint`. On the 5,000-file tree a one-file edit costs under 600 ms.

findings.title: Golden recall MRR is 0.830, not the documented 0.853, since the first consolidation created stats/ml.json
findings.evidence:
docs/BUILD_STATUS.md: `recall@5 0.781, MRR 0.853`; the test docstring says the same and fails below 0.823.
Ran the test's own scoring on the copy (BRAIN_NOW=2026-11-10T12:00:00Z):
`with learned multiplier (as the test runs it): (0.781, 0.83)`
`without multiplier: (0.781, 0.853)`
`distinct multipliers in use: [1.0, 1.3]`
engine/recall.py:350 returns TOP_MULTIPLIER (1.3) for every owner-stated item as soon as stats/ml.json exists (commit 790084d), while every other item scores 1.0 because no credit has been recorded. So with zero learned evidence, owner items get a 30% boost on every query; that costs 0.023 MRR and leaves 0.007 of margin before the regression test fails. Related plan items: learning-11 and learning-12.
findings.proposed_fix: Make the owner rule a floor instead of a constant: an owner-stated item gets the highest multiplier any other candidate has for this query (1.0 while no credit exists), never 1.3 by default. Correct the figure in BUILD_STATUS. Have the golden test pin the learned state it scores with (a fixture ml.json or none) so the number does not move when the brain learns.
findings.acceptance: With the real stats/ml.json, the golden scoring returns MRR of at least 0.853. A test with one credited lesson (multiplier 1.2) shows an owner-stated item is never ranked below it at equal relevance. BUILD_STATUS and the test docstring state the number the test measures.

findings.title: Every consolidated record is stored twice and never pruned: about 7 KB of git history per session
findings.evidence: After consolidating 300 synthetic sessions (1,800 records) in a copy: `inbox files 303 796173` (consumed files stay), `deltas 1406924 2` (the ML_FOLD operation embeds every record again), `stats/ml.json 136358`, of which `'seen': 30000` bytes for 1,500 ids (one id per record, kept forever), `stats/ledger 166121`. That is about 2.3 MB per 300 sessions, or 7.8 KB per session, in a repository cloned at the start of every chat. Time is not affected yet: boot, learn status and ml report stayed at about 140 ms.
findings.proposed_fix: Let a delta reference inbox records by file and id instead of embedding them, or delete consumed inbox files once their delta is committed (one copy either way; `learn verify` must still replay). Keep `seen` only for inbox files that still exist, or as a Bloom-style fixed-size set. Prune through a delta operation, so the pipeline remains the only writer.
findings.acceptance: After the 300-session synthetic run, `du -sb learning stats` is at most 1.2 MB (2.5 MB today) and `brain learn verify` still passes on the replay fixtures. `stats/ml.json` grows by less than 5 KB between session 300 and session 600.

findings.title: Idea: record each brain call (command, milliseconds, bytes printed) so the next audit ranks by measured use
findings.evidence: No call frequencies exist: the ranking in this report had to assume counts. The transcript scan was not usable as a baseline because calls are chained with other shell commands (for example `cat docs/NEXT_SESSION.md; ... brain plan schedule ... | head -60` returned 9,607 B, mostly not from the brain).
findings.proposed_fix: In bin/brain main(), wrap stdout with a byte counter and append one JSON line per call (command, subcommand, ms, bytes, exit) to `.brain/log/calls.jsonl` in a managed project (git-ignored like run logs), or to the temp folder otherwise. `brain ledger` adds one line: `brain output this session: N calls, about X tokens; largest: ...`. `brain close` folds the per-command totals into the run record.
findings.acceptance: After ten mixed calls in a fixture project, calls.jsonl has ten rows whose byte counts equal the captured stdout sizes, and `brain ledger` prints the one-line total. Overhead per call is under 2 ms.

findings.title: Idea: a `brain perf` self-benchmark with stored baselines, and byte caps as tests for the frequent commands
findings.evidence: Only boot has a byte cap test (1,500 B). Nothing would have caught the 85 s schedule, the 240 ms start-up or a new line added to `run`. The driver used for this audit is about 40 lines of standard library (tools/bench.py: perf_counter around subprocess, median of 5, bytes of stdout plus stderr).
findings.proposed_fix: Add `brain perf` (or `doctor --perf`): build a scratch project in a temp folder, run the frequent commands five times, print ms and bytes per command, compare bytes with `evals/perf_baseline.json`, and exit 1 when a command's bytes grow more than 25% or the 200-ticket schedule exceeds 5 s. Add deterministic byte-cap tests for run (ok and failed), gate, resume, recall, checkpoint and hr hire. Time limits stay out of unit tests (machine-dependent) except the schedule work bound.
findings.acceptance: `brain perf` prints a table and exits 0 on the current tree. Adding a 200-byte line to the run digest makes it exit 1 and name the command.

findings.title: Idea: a labelled set of failing logs that scores the digest on 'cause shown' and bytes
findings.evidence: The recall design is guarded by 60 labelled queries; the digest, which runs far more often, has no such set. The four cases built here already separate the current digest (cause shown in 2 of 4) from the prototype (4 of 4).
findings.proposed_fix: Create `evals/run_logs/` with 15-20 real-shaped failing outputs (unittest, pytest, jest, vitest, tsc, eslint, go test, cargo, npm install failure, a Python crash, a shell `command not found`, a timeout), each with the strings a lead needs. Add `brain eval digest`, reporting cause-shown rate and median bytes. Keep the failure patterns as a small data table so a new tool is a data change with a fixture.
findings.acceptance: `brain eval digest` reports at least 90% cause-shown at a median of at most 700 B, and a test fails if either number regresses.

findings.title: Idea: `plan schedule` prints the next wave, not the timeline
findings.evidence: On the 200-ticket plan the default output is 605 B: 13 start-time lines (`t=0 A1 T-022 (45) | A2 T-032 (45) | ...` through t=210), `... 139 more start times (use --json)`, the makespan line and a tokens line. `--json` is 12,471 B. A lead acts only on which tickets to start now and what they block.
findings.proposed_fix: Default output: one line with the tickets that can start now (up to the agent count) with their owned files, one line with what becomes ready after each of them, and the makespan line. Keep the full timeline behind `--timeline` and `--json`.
findings.acceptance: On the 200-ticket fixture the default output is at most 300 B and names exactly the tickets with no unfinished dependency chosen for t=0; `--timeline` reproduces today's output.
